Pregnancy

Miscarriage risk by week: what the numbers can tell you

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

It is understandable to want a reassuring number during early pregnancy, especially after a previous loss. Miscarriage becomes less likely as a pregnancy progresses, but a week alone cannot predict an individual outcome. The meaning of a percentage depends on which pregnancies were studied and what a scan has already shown.

What miscarriage figures actually measure

Miscarriage means a pregnancy ends before a locally defined gestational limit: many studies use before 20 weeks, while UK guidance uses before 24 weeks. Most losses occur in the first trimester. Estimates also differ according to whether they count all conceptions, pregnancies recognised by a positive test, or pregnancies already shown to be developing on ultrasound. Very early unrecognised losses are often missing from statistics.

The proportion of all miscarriages occurring early is different from the chance that an ongoing pregnancy will miscarry from today onward. Neither a general first-trimester estimate nor a later-pregnancy percentage is a personal forecast. There is no medically required week for announcing a pregnancy; you can choose when and with whom to share it according to the support you want.

Chromosomes, age and previous pregnancies

A typical embryo has 46 chromosomes, with 23 contributed by each parent. Errors involving missing or extra chromosome material can occur as eggs, sperm or the embryo develop. Chromosome abnormalities account for about half of miscarriages and are usually a chance event, even when both parents have normal chromosomes. The chance increases with maternal age, particularly from the mid-30s and more substantially in the 40s; fixed claims of a 75% increase or fivefold risk cannot be applied without their study population and comparison group.

One miscarriage does not mean another is inevitable. Previous losses and previous live births both help a clinician assess the next pregnancy alongside age and medical history, but a past live birth is not a guarantee. Recurrent miscarriage definitions and referral thresholds vary: RCOG defines three early losses, including non-consecutive losses, while assessment after two may be appropriate depending on the history and local guidance. Many people have a successful pregnancy even when recurrent loss remains unexplained.

Infections: different risks, not a single explanation

Infections relevant to pregnancy include Listeria, parvovirus B19, Toxoplasma gondii, rubella, herpes simplex and cytomegalovirus (CMV). These infections can affect pregnancy, but they do not all carry the same miscarriage risk. Listeriosis, toxoplasmosis and rubella can cause pregnancy loss; parvovirus can sometimes cause fetal anaemia and loss, although most exposed or infected pregnancies are not affected. CMV can harm fetal development, and genital herpes is especially important because of infection of the baby around birth; neither should be presented as a routine explanation for every early loss.

Contact your maternity team promptly after a concerning exposure, new rash, fever or genital sores. Testing and treatment depend on the infection, symptoms, timing and immunity. Repeated loss alone does not justify indiscriminate infection panels or preventive antibiotics without a specific indication. Food safety, hand hygiene and appropriate vaccination advice help reduce some risks; the live MMR vaccine is not given during pregnancy.

Uterine shape, clotting and other medical factors

Some differences in the shape of the uterus, or particular fibroids or scar tissue, can affect pregnancy. They do not mean a healthy pregnancy is impossible. Their importance depends on the exact finding, and surgery is not automatically beneficial. Diabetes or thyroid disease may also need review; well-controlled disease does not carry the same risk as poorly controlled disease.

Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is an acquired condition associated with pregnancy complications and abnormal clotting. Lupus anticoagulant is one of the antibodies assessed for APS, not a separate diagnosis proved by one blood result. Persistent laboratory findings and the clinical history matter. Inherited thrombophilias are different: routine testing or treatment for them is not recommended for unexplained recurrent early loss. Do not start aspirin, heparin or other treatments yourself; selected patients with confirmed APS may benefit from specialist treatment.

Before six weeks: get the dating right

Pregnancy weeks are usually counted from the first day of the last menstrual period. In a typical cycle, the first two weeks on that calendar occur before conception. A claim that miscarriage happens in pregnancy week one or two therefore confuses menstrual dating with time since conception. Ovulation varies, and a dating scan may revise the estimate.

After conception, a very early loss can occur before someone realises they are pregnant, sometimes around an expected or delayed period. This is one reason risk figures before six weeks are difficult to compare. A single early scan may be too soon to establish viability; follow-up testing or a repeat scan may be needed. Do not use a calendar estimate alone to diagnose loss.

Six to twelve weeks: what a heartbeat study showed

A 2008 Australian study followed 696 asymptomatic women after an ultrasound showed cardiac activity in a singleton pregnancy at their first visit between 6 weeks 2 days and 11 weeks 6 days. The subsequent miscarriage proportions were 9.4% after a visit at six completed weeks, 4.2% at seven, 1.5% at eight, 0.5% at nine and 0.7% at ten. These were remaining risks of loss before 20 weeks after that visit, not the risk in each individual week or a ten-percentage-point reduction caused by seeing a heartbeat.

These older observations describe a selected group with reassuring scan findings and no symptoms; only 11 losses occurred. They are not a universal calculator for bleeding, recurrent miscarriage, multiple pregnancy or every age group. The small rise from nine to ten weeks does not establish a biological increase in risk. Discuss your own scan, dates, symptoms and history with your clinician rather than attaching certainty to a decimal.

Thirteen to twenty weeks and beyond

Risk generally falls as a pregnancy continues, and later miscarriage is less common than early miscarriage. It does not settle at a universal 5% at twelve weeks or stay above a fixed 5% floor thereafter. Different studies use different gestational limits, populations and starting points; a second-trimester estimate cannot be substituted for the remaining risk after a normal twelve-week scan.

A reassuring scan cannot rule out every later complication. Continue antenatal appointments and seek advice about new bleeding, pain, fluid loss or other concerns. Your team may recommend additional monitoring for a particular history or diagnosis. The transition between miscarriage and other forms of pregnancy loss also depends on local definitions, so statistics ending at 20 and 24 weeks should not be treated as equivalent.

Bleeding and pain: when to get help

Bleeding and cramps in the abdomen, pelvis or lower back can accompany miscarriage, but they can also occur in continuing pregnancies. Some losses cause no obvious symptoms and are found on a scan. Brown or dark-red spotting does not prove that everything is safe, and bright-red blood does not by itself diagnose loss. Get same-day advice from a maternity or early-pregnancy service for any bleeding or spotting during pregnancy, even without pain, or for fluid loss or unusual discharge.

Seek immediate emergency care for heavy bleeding that soaks a pad soon after putting it on, severe abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain, marked dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness. One-sided pelvic pain with possible pregnancy needs urgent assessment because of ectopic pregnancy, even without a positive test; severe pain or faintness is an emergency. Ultrasound and sometimes blood tests establish what is happening. An early uncertain result may need follow-up: colour, cramps and a risk chart cannot confirm the diagnosis.

Supporting health without blaming yourself

Most early losses cannot be prevented by something you do differently. They are not evidence that you failed to rest, think positively or protect the pregnancy. A balanced diet, appropriate regular activity, avoiding smoking, alcohol and recreational drugs, limiting total caffeine to no more than 200 mg daily, and attending antenatal care support health without guaranteeing an outcome. Routine bed rest is not a way to prevent miscarriage; activity advice should be individualised if there is a specific complication.

Review existing conditions, medicines, food safety and recommended supplements with your team before pregnancy or as early as possible. Do not stop prescribed medicine or start hormones, blood thinners or unproven supplements on your own. Anxiety after loss deserves support too. You can ask for counselling, practical support and a plan for contact or scans in a future pregnancy, without being promised that extra monitoring prevents every loss.

When investigations or genetic counselling may help

After repeated loss, assessment starts with the pregnancy, personal and family history. Depending on the situation it may include uterine imaging, APS and thyroid tests, selected diabetes testing, or chromosome testing of pregnancy tissue. Testing one or both parents' chromosomes or arranging genetic counselling may be appropriate after a relevant tissue result or an individual risk assessment; a broad genetic blood panel for every couple is not the default.

Ask when referral is appropriate after two or more losses, especially with a later loss, known medical condition or relevant family history. Tests do not always find a cause, and treatment is directed at an established indication rather than a risk percentage alone. A previous loss can remain emotionally significant even when the next pregnancy's outlook is good; support and careful explanations are part of care, not something you have to earn by reaching a particular number of losses.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Current NHS and RCOG guidance informs symptom triage and recurrent-loss assessment. The Irish guideline is labelled June 2025; its version history records a March 2026 update.

Week-specific heartbeat figures come from the original 2008 Australian observational study, not a new guideline or an individual risk calculator.

Gestational definitions and referral thresholds vary between services; an access date does not make an older publication newly updated.

How BeMama can help

BeMama explains population figures and questions for a clinical appointment; it does not calculate an individual's miscarriage risk or diagnose pregnancy loss.

When to seek help

Get same-day advice for any pregnancy bleeding or spotting. Seek immediate emergency care for heavy bleeding, severe abdominal or shoulder-tip pain, marked dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness. Do not let a reassuring percentage delay assessment or start hormones, aspirin or heparin without a prescription.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A percentage only makes sense with its population, starting point and definition of loss.
  • Risk generally falls with advancing pregnancy, but there is no fixed 5% floor or universal heartbeat guarantee.
  • Any pregnancy bleeding needs same-day advice; heavy bleeding, severe pain, shoulder pain or faintness need immediate emergency care.
  • Most early losses are beyond personal control; investigations and treatments should follow the history and a clear clinical indication.

Frequently asked questions

Which infections can affect miscarriage risk?

Listeria, toxoplasma and rubella can cause pregnancy loss, and parvovirus B19 can sometimes cause fetal anaemia and loss. CMV and herpes also matter in pregnancy, but their risks differ and they are not interchangeable explanations for early miscarriage. Ask promptly about symptoms or exposure; do not self-order broad panels or take preventive antibiotics.

What is the risk between six and twelve weeks after a heartbeat is seen?

It depends on the pregnancy. In the selected asymptomatic singleton group studied in 2008, remaining loss before 20 weeks after a reassuring visit was 9.4% at six completed weeks, then 4.2%, 1.5%, 0.5% and 0.7% at visits at seven, eight, nine and ten weeks. These older figures are not a personal prediction or a ten-point reduction for everyone.

Does risk stay at 5% from thirteen to twenty weeks?

No. Risk usually decreases as pregnancy progresses, but there is no universal 5% minimum after twelve weeks. A study's starting point, population, scan findings and definition of miscarriage change the estimate. Later symptoms still need assessment.

Can I prevent a miscarriage?

Most early losses cannot be prevented. Healthy eating, suitable activity, antenatal visits, avoiding smoking, alcohol and recreational drugs, and keeping caffeine at or below 200 mg daily support health. They cannot guarantee prevention, and a miscarriage is not your fault.

Can miscarriage happen in the first two pregnancy weeks?

With usual last-period dating, those weeks are generally before conception. Very early loss occurs after conception and may pass unrecognised around a period. Menstrual weeks and weeks since conception are different.

Are a few brown spots safe to ignore?

No. Colour and amount alone cannot show that a pregnancy is safe or diagnose miscarriage. Get same-day advice for any pregnancy spotting or bleeding. Heavy bleeding, severe abdominal or shoulder-tip pain, dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness need immediate emergency care.

Does one loss mean I need extensive genetic tests?

Usually not. The history guides testing; many early chromosome errors are chance events. Repeated losses, a relevant family history or a pregnancy-tissue finding may lead to selected tests or genetic counselling. Discuss referral rather than assuming a standard panel fits everyone.

Will a uterine difference or clotting result prevent a healthy pregnancy?

Not necessarily. Many people with uterine differences have healthy pregnancies. An isolated antibody result does not establish APS, and inherited thrombophilia is a separate issue. Assessment and any treatment depend on the exact diagnosis, history and specialist advice.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
